title: Flame Test

experiment.name: Flame Test for Identifying Metal Ions
experiment.category: Qualitative Analysis / Metals and their Compounds
experiment.objective: To identify the metal ion present in a salt sample by observing the characteristic colour it imparts to a non-luminous (blue) Bunsen flame when a small amount of the salt is introduced into the flame.
experiment.description: A Bunsen/blow torch is mounted on a stand and lit with a non-luminous blue flame, held steady by one hand. With the other hand, a small amount of the salt sample is held in a pair of tongs (or on a wire loop) and introduced into the hot blue flame. The heat excites the electrons of the metal ions; as they fall back to lower energy levels they emit light of a characteristic colour. A watch glass holding the powdered sample sits on the wooden bench below, and fine particles/vapour stream down from the flame toward it. The colour seen in the flame identifies the metal ion.

procedure: Place the apparatus on a heat-resistant wooden bench.
Light the Bunsen burner / torch and adjust it to give a non-luminous blue flame.
Take a small amount of the salt sample from the watch glass using clean tongs (or a wire loop).
Introduce the sample into the hottest part of the blue flame.
Observe the colour imparted to the flame.
Match the observed colour with the characteristic flame colour of known metal ions to identify the ion present.
Clean the tongs / loop before testing another sample to avoid contamination.

principle.concept: Excitation and emission of light by metal ions (atomic emission)
principle.explanation: When a metal salt is heated in a hot flame, the thermal energy excites the outer electrons of the metal ions to higher energy levels. These excited electrons are unstable and fall back to lower energy levels, releasing the absorbed energy as light of specific wavelengths. The combination of wavelengths gives each metal ion a characteristic flame colour, which can be used to identify it.
principle.key_difference: Different metal ions have different electron energy-level spacings, so each emits light of a characteristic colour — this is what makes the flame test diagnostic.

conclusion: The colour imparted to a non-luminous flame by a heated salt is characteristic of the metal ion it contains, because excited electrons emit light of specific wavelengths as they return to lower energy levels. The flame test is therefore a simple qualitative method to identify metal ions in a sample.
properties_demonstrated: Characteristic flame colours of metal ions
Excitation and emission of light by atoms
Qualitative identification of metals by flame colour
precautions: Always use a non-luminous (blue) flame so the flame's own colour does not mask the sample colour.
Use clean tongs or a clean wire loop for each sample to avoid contamination (especially by sodium, which masks other colours).
Hold the sample in the hottest part of the flame for a clear colour.
Do not look directly into the flame for long; observe the colour from the side.
Keep the sample amount small and handle the hot apparatus with care.
